# **1\. Introduction & Scope**

## **1.1 Purpose**

This document specifies the design of a hand-written CSS parser implemented in Rust. It defines the tokenizer and parser architecture, the abstract syntax tree (AST) the parser produces, and the boundary of CSS syntax the parser is responsible for. It is written to be implementable directly: every stage below maps to a concrete Rust module, and every grammar rule is either shown as a railroad diagram sourced from the authoritative specification or as an explicit Rust type.

The project targets what the accompanying research phase called an “80% CSS parser”: a parser that correctly tokenizes and structurally parses the overwhelming majority of real-world CSS — rules, at-rules, declarations, selectors, and values — without attempting full conformance with every CSS module ever published. Section 8 draws an explicit line between what is in scope and what is deliberately deferred.

## **1.2 Goals & Non-Goals**

**Goals** — the parser should:

* Tokenize CSS input according to the CSS Syntax Module Level 3 grammar, including all 18 token types, escapes, and error tokens.

* Parse a token/component-value stream into a generic, syntax-level AST (stylesheets, at-rules, qualified rules, declarations, component values) following the spec's parser algorithms.

* Support CSS Nesting (nested style rules and the “&” selector) as a first-class part of the grammar, not a bolt-on.

* Recover from syntax errors the way real user agents do — by discarding only the smallest enclosing construct — rather than aborting the whole parse.

* Provide a selectors sub-parser and a values sub-parser that cover the constructs developers actually write day to day (combinators, attribute selectors, An+B, calc(), var(), color functions, comma/space-separated lists).

* Be a good citizen of the Rust ecosystem: no \`unsafe\`, predictable allocation behavior, and a public API that is pleasant to build tooling on top of (linters, formatters, minifiers).

**Non-goals** — the parser explicitly does not attempt to:

* Validate that a declaration's value matches its property's specific value grammar (that is the job of each CSS module's own spec, not the Syntax module).

* Evaluate @media / @supports conditions against a real environment, or resolve var() substitutions against a cascade.

* Implement the full CSSOM, cascade, specificity, or computed-value pipeline.

* Chase every CSS proposal at every draft stage; the parser targets broadly-implemented, Candidate-Recommendation-or-later syntax.

## **1.3 Relationship to the CSS Syntax Module Level 3**

The CSS Working Group deliberately separates *how CSS is written down* (the Syntax module) from *what any particular piece of CSS means* (Selectors, Values & Units, and every property-bearing module). This specification follows that same separation: Sections 4 and 5 below implement the Syntax module's tokenizer and parser algorithms essentially one-to-one, producing a **generic** tree of tokens, functions, and blocks. Section 6 then layers a thin, opinionated interpretation of that generic tree for selectors and values — enough to be useful, without trying to re-implement every downstream module.

The tokenizer and parser algorithms, and the non-normative railroad diagrams reproduced in Section 4.3, are sourced from [CSS Syntax Module Level 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-syntax-3/) (W3C Candidate Recommendation Draft). The diagrams in this document are freshly generated from that grammar using the same open-source railroad-diagram generator the spec's own editors use, rather than being screenshots of the spec — see the note at the start of Section 4.3.

## **1.4 Document Conventions**

* Grammar diagrams: *railroad diagrams* read left to right along the top track; branches below are alternatives; loops indicate repetition. Green rounded boxes are literal characters or character classes; blue rectangular boxes are references to another diagram or production defined elsewhere in this document.

* Code: all code samples are Rust (edition 2021\) and are meant as an interface sketch — signatures and types are load-bearing, function bodies are illustrative.

* Spec cross-references like §5.4.2 refer to section numbers in CSS Syntax Module Level 3, for traceability back to the normative source.

# **2\. Architecture Overview**

The parser is organized as a strict pipeline with a hard boundary between lexical analysis and grammar. Each stage consumes the previous stage's output and has a single, narrow responsibility, which keeps error recovery, testing, and incremental re-parsing tractable.

![][image1]

*Figure 2.1 — Parser pipeline. Diagram generated for this document; not a spec figure.*

## **2.1 Stage responsibilities**

| Stage | Input | Output | Responsibility |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Preprocess | Raw byte / UTF-8 stream | Filtered code points | Normalize newlines (CR, CRLF, FF → LF); replace NUL and surrogates with U+FFFD. |
| Tokenizer | Code points | Token stream (on demand) | Implements §4 — turns characters into the 18 CSS token types, resolving escapes and numeric literals. |
| Parser | Tokens / component values | Generic CSS AST | Implements §5 — groups tokens into functions, simple blocks, declarations, qualified rules, and at-rules, with panic-mode error recovery. |
| Selectors / Values | Component-value slices from the AST | Selector lists, value trees | Opinionated but partial interpretation layer described in Section 6; not part of the Syntax module. |

## **2.2 Why a generic AST first**

A recurring theme in the design research behind this project is that mature CSS engines (Blink, and Servo/Mozilla's cssparser) first build a *generic* tree — tokens, functions, and {}/()/\[\] blocks — and only interpret it against a specific grammar (a selector list, a property's value grammar, a media-query list) when something downstream asks for it. This project follows the same approach for two concrete reasons:

* Forward compatibility: new at-rules, new pseudo-classes, and new value syntax parse structurally even before this crate knows what they mean, exactly as the spec requires user agents to do.

* Testability: the tokenizer and syntax-level parser can be fully conformance-tested against the CSS Syntax Module's own test suite (Section 10\) independent of how much of Selectors/Values Level 4 this crate has chosen to interpret.

# **3\. Design Rationale**

## **3.1 Parsing strategy: recursive descent vs. PEG vs. LR**

Three broad families of parsing strategy were evaluated during the research phase. The comparison below focuses on the properties that matter most for CSS specifically: tolerance of a mostly-deterministic but occasionally context-sensitive grammar, and the ability to implement the spec's own error-recovery rules without fighting the parsing framework.

| Criterion | Recursive descent (LL) | Packrat (PEG) | LR / LALR (generator-based) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Performance | O(n) typical; hand control over backtracking | Guaranteed O(n) via memoization | Guaranteed O(n) |
| Memory | Low — call-stack only | High — memo table is O(input × grammar) | Moderate — parse stack |
| Error recovery | Easy to hand-code the spec's exact resync rules | Awkward — backtracking obscures the failure point | Poor — generic, generator-produced messages |
| Left recursion | Rewritten as loops (selectors, combinators) | Disallowed without a special extension | Native support |
| Fit for CSS's mixed contexts | Good — custom properties, nesting, nth-child()-microsyntax are easy to special-case | Good grammar expressivity, but memo cost is hard to justify for a browser/tooling workload | CFG purity fights CSS's deliberately informal, forgiving grammar |

This project uses **hand-written recursive descent**, matching the approach used by Blink's CSSParserImpl and Servo's cssparser. CSS's own spec is written as a set of mutually-recursive “consume a …” algorithms operating on a token stream — recursive descent is close to a direct transcription of that spec, which minimizes the chance of subtly diverging from it. Packrat's automatic backtracking is not needed because CSS's grammar rarely requires more than one token of lookahead once component values are grouped; and LR generators fight the spec's context-sensitive constructs (custom properties, \<any-value\>, nesting) more than they help.

## **3.2 Lexer / parser separation**

The spec itself supports two valid implementation shapes: a fully separate tokenizer that materializes a token list, or an integrated scanner-parser that tokenizes on demand (cssparser takes the latter approach). This project uses **on-demand tokenization**: the Tokenizer exposes a next\_token method and the parser is written against a peekable iterator over it, rather than eagerly collecting a Vec\<Token\>. This avoids allocating and holding an entire token buffer for large stylesheets, and it mirrors the way the spec itself defines tokenization — as a callable, single-token-at-a-time algorithm (§4.3.1) — rather than as a batch transform.

## **3.3 Why Rust**

The implementation-language trade-off was evaluated against C, the language of most production CSS engines (Blink, Lexbor, libcroco). The deciding factors for this project:

* **Memory safety without a GC.** Arena-style AST allocation is still idiomatic in Rust (e.g. via bumpalo), but use-after-free and buffer-overrun classes of bugs that plague hand-rolled C parsers are eliminated at compile time.

* **Sum types model CSS's grammar directly.** A CSS component value is a closed, small set of alternatives (a token, a function, or one of three block kinds) — exactly what a Rust enum is for. The equivalent C code needs a tagged union and manual discriminant management.

* **Ecosystem fit.** Prior art exists to validate design decisions against (cssparser, selectors), without requiring this project to depend on them — see Section 7.4.

* **Tooling.** cargo, rustfmt, clippy, cargo-fuzz, and Miri materially lower the cost of the testing strategy in Section 10\.

The trade-off accepted: Rust's borrow checker adds friction to code that copies substrings out of the input and hands them to a caller with a different lifetime; the interface sketches in this document use Cow\<'a, str\> (allocate only when an escape sequence forces it) as the default answer to that friction — see Section 7.2.

# **4\. Tokenization Specification**

## **4.1 Input preprocessing**

Before tokenization, the input byte stream is decoded to Unicode code points and filtered per CSS Syntax §3.2–3.3: CR, FF, and CRLF sequences are normalized to a single LF, and any NUL or surrogate code point is replaced with U+FFFD. For v1, this crate assumes the input is already valid UTF-8 (the overwhelmingly common case on the web and in tooling); charset-label sniffing and BOM-driven fallback-encoding detection (full §3.2) are tracked as a v2 stretch goal rather than blocking the core parser — see Section 8\.

## **4.2 Token type inventory**

| Token | Carries | Example |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| \<ident-token\> | value: Cow\<str\> | flex, \--my-var, sans-serif |
| \<function-token\> | name: Cow\<str\> | calc(, translate( |
| \<at-keyword-token\> | value: Cow\<str\> | @media, @font-face |
| \<hash-token\> | value: Cow\<str\>, id flag | \#header, \#ff0000 |
| \<string-token\> / \<bad-string-token\> | value: Cow\<str\> | "Helvetica Neue" |
| \<url-token\> / \<bad-url-token\> | value: Cow\<str\> | url(a.png) |
| \<number-token\> | value: f64, integer flag | 42, \-3.14, 6.02e23 |
| \<percentage-token\> | value: f64 | 50% |
| \<dimension-token\> | value: f64, unit: Cow\<str\> | 16px, 2.5rem |
| \<delim-token\> | value: char | \+, \>, \~, . |
| \<whitespace-token\> | — | (run of space / tab / newline) |
| \<CDO-token\> / \<CDC-token\> | — | \<\!--  /  \--\> |
| \<colon-token\> / \<semicolon-token\> / \<comma-token\> | — | :  ;  , |
| \<(-token\> \<)-token\> \<\[-token\> \<\]-token\> \<{-token\> \<}-token\> | — | ( ) \[ \] { } |
| \<EOF-token\> | — | (end of input; never appears in source) |

## **4.3 Token Railroad Diagrams**

The 18 diagrams below reproduce the grammar in [CSS Syntax Module Level 3 §4.1, “Token Railroad Diagrams”](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-syntax-3/#token-diagrams). Per the spec, these diagrams are *non-normative and incomplete* — they describe the shape of a well-formed token but not the tokenizer's error-handling behavior (that lives in the prose algorithms of §4.3, summarized as Rust in Section 4.4). Each diagram here was freshly generated for this document from the grammar structure using the same open-source railroad-diagrams generator library its original author (Tab Atkins, co-editor of this spec) publishes — not copied as an image from the spec page — so the visual language (green rounded boxes for literal text/character classes, blue rectangular boxes for references to another production) is faithful to the source while the artwork itself is original to this document.

***4.3.1  comment***

![][image2]

*Figure 4.1 — comment*

/\* ... \*/. Consumed and discarded during tokenization — comments never become part of the token stream (§4.3.2).

***4.3.2  newline***

![][image3]

*Figure 4.2 — newline*

A single logical newline. CR, CRLF, and FF are all normalized to LF during preprocessing (§3.3), so the tokenizer itself only ever observes LF.

***4.3.3  whitespace***

![][image4]

*Figure 4.3 — whitespace*

One space, tab, or newline code point.

***4.3.4  hex digit***

![][image5]

*Figure 4.4 — hex digit*

0–9, a–f, or A–F — used by escapes and by nothing else at the token-diagram level.

***4.3.5  escape***

![][image6]

*Figure 4.5 — escape*

A backslash followed by either one code point that is not a newline or hex digit, or by one to six hex digits (optionally followed by one whitespace code point that terminates the escape without being part of it).

***4.3.6  \<whitespace-token\>***

![][image7]

*Figure 4.6 — \<whitespace-token\>*

One or more consecutive whitespace code points, collapsed into a single token.

***4.3.7  ws\****

![][image8]

*Figure 4.7 — ws\**

Zero or more \<whitespace-token\>s. This production, not a token itself, appears throughout the rest of the grammar wherever incidental whitespace is permitted and ignored.

***4.3.8  \<ident-token\>***

![][image9]

*Figure 4.8 — \<ident-token\>*

Identifiers, keywords, and custom-property names. May start with “--” (custom properties), an optional single “-”, and then an ident-start code point or escape, followed by zero or more ident code points or escapes.

***4.3.9  \<function-token\>***

![][image10]

*Figure 4.9 — \<function-token\>*

An \<ident-token\> immediately followed by “(” with no space — e.g. calc(, var(, url(.

***4.3.10  \<at-keyword-token\>***

![][image11]

*Figure 4.10 — \<at-keyword-token\>*

“@” immediately followed by an \<ident-token\> — e.g. @media, @supports, @font-face.

***4.3.11  \<hash-token\>***

![][image12]

*Figure 4.11 — \<hash-token\>*

“\#” followed by one or more name code points or escapes. Carries an “id” vs. “unrestricted” type flag (used to distinguish ID selectors from hex colors) that this diagram, being non-normative, doesn't show.

***4.3.12  \<string-token\>***

![][image13]

*Figure 4.12 — \<string-token\>*

A double- or single-quoted string. An escaped newline inside the quotes is consumed as a line continuation rather than ending the string.

***4.3.13  \<url-token\>***

![][image14]

*Figure 4.13 — \<url-token\>*

The unquoted contents of a url(...) call: optional leading/trailing whitespace around a run of characters that are not quotes, parens, backslash, whitespace, or a non-printable code point (or an escape).

***4.3.14  \<number-token\>***

![][image15]

*Figure 4.14 — \<number-token\>*

An optional sign, an integer and/or fractional part (at least one digit somewhere), and an optional exponent.

***4.3.15  \<dimension-token\>***

![][image16]

*Figure 4.15 — \<dimension-token\>*

A \<number-token\> immediately followed by an \<ident-token\> unit — e.g. 12px, 1.5rem, 90deg.

***4.3.16  \<percentage-token\>***

![][image17]

*Figure 4.16 — \<percentage-token\>*

A \<number-token\> immediately followed by “%”.

***4.3.17  \<CDO-token\>***

![][image18]

*Figure 4.17 — \<CDO-token\>*

The literal four characters \<\!-- — a legacy HTML-comment-hiding marker, valid only at the top level of a stylesheet.

***4.3.18  \<CDC-token\>***

![][image19]

*Figure 4.18 — \<CDC-token\>*

The literal three characters \--\> — the closing counterpart to \<CDO-token\>.

# **5\. Grammar & Parsing Specification**

## **5.1 Parser entry points**

CSS Syntax §5.3 defines several named entry points into the parser, each used by a different downstream caller. This crate exposes one public method per entry point rather than a single generic “parse” function, since each has a distinct return type and failure mode.

| Entry point (spec name) | Used for | Crate API |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Parse a stylesheet | A full .css file | Parser::parse\_stylesheet(\&mut self) \-\> Stylesheet |
| Parse a list of rules | @media / @supports / @layer block contents | Parser::parse\_rule\_list(\&mut self) \-\> Vec\<Rule\> |
| Parse a rule | Single-rule insertion (CSSOM-style) | Parser::parse\_rule(\&mut self) \-\> Result\<Rule, ParseError\> |
| Parse a declaration | @supports (prop: value) conditions | Parser::parse\_declaration(\&mut self) \-\> Result\<Declaration, ParseError\> |
| Parse a list of declarations | style="..." attributes; @page / @font-face bodies | Parser::parse\_declaration\_list(\&mut self) \-\> Vec\<DeclarationOrAtRule\> |
| Parse a style block’s contents | Nesting-aware qualified-rule bodies | Parser::parse\_style\_block(\&mut self) \-\> (Vec\<Declaration\>, Vec\<Rule\>) |
| Parse a (comma-separated) list of component values | Selector lists, media-query lists | Parser::parse\_component\_value\_list(\&mut self) \[ \_comma\_separated variant \] |

## **5.2 Core consume algorithms**

The parser itself is a set of mutually recursive functions, one per “consume a …” algorithm in CSS Syntax §5.4. Below is an interface sketch: real signatures and the behavior each is responsible for, written directly against this crate's Token/ComponentValue types from Section 5.3. The step-by-step control flow inside each function should be transcribed from the spec's own numbered steps rather than re-derived from this summary — the spec's exact ordering (e.g. checking for a {\-token before falling through to the generic “anything else” branch) encodes error-handling subtleties that are easy to lose when paraphrasing.

/// Entry point for rule parsing. Repeatedly consumes rules until EOF.  
/// \`top\_level\` controls how stray \<CDO-token\>/\<CDC-token\> are handled:  
/// ignored at the true top level of a stylesheet, but treated as the  
/// start of a qualified rule when nested (e.g. inside @media).  
fn consume\_list\_of\_rules(\&mut self, top\_level: bool) \-\> Vec\<Rule\<'i\>\> { .. }  
   
/// Consumes one at-rule. Assumes the current token is already the  
/// \<at-keyword-token\>. Collects component values into the prelude  
/// until a \<;-token\> (statement form), a \<{-token\> (block form), or EOF.  
fn consume\_at\_rule(\&mut self) \-\> AtRule\<'i\> { .. }  
   
/// Consumes one qualified rule (a style rule, in the common case).  
/// Collects prelude component values until the first top-level  
/// \<{-token\>, then delegates to \`consume\_simple\_block\`. Returns \`None\`  
/// if EOF is reached before any block is found — a parse error, and  
/// per §2.2 the whole rule is then discarded rather than salvaged.  
fn consume\_qualified\_rule(\&mut self) \-\> Option\<QualifiedRule\<'i\>\> { .. }  
   
/// Nesting-aware: consumes a style rule's \`{}\` block, where both  
/// declarations \*and\* nested qualified rules are legal. An  
/// \<ident-token\> here tentatively starts a declaration; anything else  
/// (including a "&" \<delim-token\>) is reconsumed and parsed as a  
/// nested rule via \`consume\_qualified\_rule\`.  
fn consume\_style\_block\_contents(\&mut self) \-\> (Vec\<Declaration\<'i\>\>, Vec\<Rule\<'i\>\>) { .. }  
   
/// Non-nesting form used by @page, @font-face, @keyframes children,  
/// and the \`style="..."\` attribute grammar: only declarations (and,  
/// generally invalidly, at-rules) are recognized here — never a  
/// nested qualified rule.  
fn consume\_list\_of\_declarations(\&mut self) \-\> Vec\<DeclarationOrAtRule\<'i\>\> { .. }  
   
/// Consumes \`name: value\` up to (but not including) the terminating  
/// \<;-token\> / \<}-token\> / EOF, then trims a trailing \`\!important\`  
/// and any trailing whitespace off the collected value. Returns  
/// \`None\` if the first non-whitespace token after the name is not  
/// a \<:-token\> — that is a parse error, per §5.4.6.  
fn consume\_declaration(\&mut self) \-\> Option\<Declaration\<'i\>\> { .. }  
   
/// Dispatches on the current token: \<{-token\> / \<\[-token\> / \<(-token\>  
/// delegate to \`consume\_simple\_block\`; \<function-token\> delegates to  
/// \`consume\_function\`; everything else is returned unchanged as a  
/// "preserved token".  
fn consume\_component\_value(\&mut self) \-\> ComponentValue\<'i\> { .. }  
   
/// Consumes component values until the mirror of \`ending\_token\`  
/// (\`}\` for \`{\`, \`)\` for \`(\`, \`\]\` for \`\[\`) or EOF.  
fn consume\_simple\_block(\&mut self, ending\_token: \&Token\<'i\>) \-\> SimpleBlock\<'i\> { .. }  
   
/// Consumes component values until a \<)-token\> or EOF. Assumes the  
/// current token is already a \<function-token\>.  
fn consume\_function(\&mut self) \-\> Function\<'i\> { .. }

## **5.3 Generic AST**

These types are the direct Rust encoding of the objects CSS Syntax §5 defines: tokens, *preserved* into a component-value tree via functions and simple blocks, then grouped into declarations and rules. Every field below corresponds to a named property in the spec's prose (a rule's “prelude”, a declaration's “important flag”, and so on).

pub enum Token\<'i\> {  
    Ident(Cow\<'i, str\>),  
    Function(Cow\<'i, str\>),  
    AtKeyword(Cow\<'i, str\>),  
    Hash { value: Cow\<'i, str\>, is\_id: bool },  
    QuotedString(Cow\<'i, str\>),  
    BadString,  
    Url(Cow\<'i, str\>),  
    BadUrl,  
    Delim(char),  
    Number { value: f64, is\_integer: bool },  
    Percentage(f64),  
    Dimension { value: f64, is\_integer: bool, unit: Cow\<'i, str\> },  
    Whitespace,  
    Cdo,  
    Cdc,  
    Colon,  
    Semicolon,  
    Comma,  
    OpenSquare, CloseSquare,  
    OpenParen, CloseParen,  
    OpenCurly, CloseCurly,  
    Eof,  
}  
   
/// A component value is a preserved token, a function, or a block —  
/// exactly the three alternatives CSS Syntax §5.2 defines.  
pub enum ComponentValue\<'i\> {  
    Token(Token\<'i\>),  
    Function(Function\<'i\>),  
    Block(SimpleBlock\<'i\>),  
}  
   
pub struct Function\<'i\> {  
    pub name: Cow\<'i, str\>,  
    pub value: Vec\<ComponentValue\<'i\>\>,  
}  
   
pub struct SimpleBlock\<'i\> {  
    /// The opening token that started this block: \`{\`, \`(\`, or \`\[\`.  
    pub associated\_token: Token\<'i\>,  
    pub value: Vec\<ComponentValue\<'i\>\>,  
}  
   
pub struct Stylesheet\<'i\> {  
    pub rules: Vec\<Rule\<'i\>\>,  
}  
   
pub enum Rule\<'i\> {  
    At(AtRule\<'i\>),  
    Qualified(QualifiedRule\<'i\>),  
}  
   
pub struct AtRule\<'i\> {  
    pub name: Cow\<'i, str\>,  
    pub prelude: Vec\<ComponentValue\<'i\>\>,  
    /// \`None\` for statement-form at-rules, e.g. \`@import "x.css";\`.  
    pub block: Option\<SimpleBlock\<'i\>\>,  
}  
   
pub struct QualifiedRule\<'i\> {  
    pub prelude: Vec\<ComponentValue\<'i\>\>,  
    pub block: SimpleBlock\<'i\>,  
}  
   
pub enum DeclarationOrAtRule\<'i\> {  
    Declaration(Declaration\<'i\>),  
    AtRule(AtRule\<'i\>),  
}  
   
pub struct Declaration\<'i\> {  
    pub name: Cow\<'i, str\>,  
    pub value: Vec\<ComponentValue\<'i\>\>,  
    pub important: bool,  
}

## **5.4 CSS Nesting integration point**

The Nesting Module is not part of CSS Syntax Level 3, but the Syntax spec was designed with a single, deliberate integration seam for it: consume\_style\_block\_contents (§5.4.4). When that function meets an \<ident-token\>, it must tentatively try a declaration parse first; when it meets anything else — including a "&" \<delim-token\> — it reconsumes and falls through to consume\_qualified\_rule. This crate implements nesting entirely inside that one function and does not special-case & anywhere else in the syntax-level parser; relative-selector semantics for & (what it resolves to, how it composes with combinators) belong to the interpretation layer in Section 6, not to this generic parsing stage.

# **6\. Selectors & Values Interpretation Layer**

Unlike Section 5, nothing in this section is part of the CSS Syntax module. It is this crate's own opinionated second pass over the ComponentValue slices already produced — a QualifiedRule's prelude (selectors) and a Declaration's value (property values) — covering the constructs developers write *in practice*, not full per-property grammar validation (that boundary is drawn precisely in Section 8).

## **6.1 Selector grammar covered**

| Construct | Example | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Type / universal | div, \* | Plain \<ident-token\> / \<delim-token "\*"\> |
| Class / ID | .card, \#main | ID relies on \<hash-token\>'s “id” type flag from §4 |
| Attribute | \[href\], \[data-x="y" i\] | Case-sensitivity modifier (i / s) supported |
| Combinators | a \> b,  a \+ b,  a \~ b,  a b | Descendant combinator is a bare \<whitespace-token\> |
| Compound / complex lists | a.b\#c\[d\]:hover | Left recursion in the spec's grammar is rewritten as an iterative loop |
| An+B microsyntax | :nth-child(2n+1) | Dedicated sub-recognizer — see 6.3 |
| Nesting selector | &,  & \> a | An ordinary "&" \<delim-token\> at the head of a compound selector |

## **6.2 Value grammar covered**

| Construct | Example | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Scalars | 16px, 50%, red, "Arial" | Pass through as their component-value form |
| Lists | 10px 20px  /  Arial, sans-serif | Whitespace- vs. comma-separated, distinguished structurally |
| Generic functions | translate(10px, 5px) | Name \+ argument component values, always parseable |
| calc() family | calc(100% \- 2rem) | \+ \- \* / with precedence, built into an expression tree; numeric-only evaluation (see Section 8.2) |
| var() | var(--gap, 8px) | Custom-property reference plus optional \<any-value\> fallback |
| Color functions | rgb(255 0 0 / 50%), oklch(…) | Structural parse of channel component values; no gamut/channel validation |

## **6.3 The An+B microsyntax**

An+B (:nth-child() and friends) predates the current tokenizer and does not decompose cleanly into the 18 ordinary token types — spec §6 defines it directly in terms of tokens like an \<n-dimension-token\> or an \<ndashdigit-ident\> that only make sense in this one context. Rather than contort the general tokenizer, this crate recognizes An+B as a small, separate grammar over an already-tokenized component-value slice:

/// Parses the contents of an already-isolated \`:nth-\*(...)\` argument  
/// list into (A, B). Returns \`None\` if the slice doesn't match any  
/// of the productions in CSS Syntax §6.2 (including \`odd\` / \`even\`).  
fn parse\_anb(input: &\[ComponentValue\]) \-\> Option\<(i32, i32)\> { .. }

# **7\. Rust Crate Architecture**

## **7.1 Module layout**

css-parser/  
├─ Cargo.toml  
└─ src/  
   ├─ lib.rs               // public API surface  
   ├─ token.rs             // Token enum; numeric \+ ident sub-lexers  
   ├─ tokenizer.rs         // Tokenizer, §4 algorithms  
   ├─ ast.rs               // ComponentValue / Function / SimpleBlock / Rule / …  
   ├─ parser/  
   │  ├─ mod.rs            // Parser struct, entry points (§5.1)  
   │  ├─ rules.rs          // consume\_list\_of\_rules, at-rule, qualified rule  
   │  └─ declarations.rs   // consume\_declaration(\_list), style-block contents  
   ├─ selectors.rs         // Section 6.1  
   ├─ values.rs            // Section 6.2 (calc, var, color, list handling)  
   ├─ anb.rs               // An+B microsyntax (§6.3)  
   ├─ error.rs             // ParseError, Diagnostics, recovery helpers  
   └─ span.rs              // byte-offset Span type attached to tokens/nodes

## **7.2 String ownership: Cow\<str\> over the input buffer**

The Tokenizer\<'i\> borrows the input as &'i str, and tokens carry Cow\<'i, str\> rather than an owned String: an ident, string, or URL with no escape sequences (the overwhelming common case) borrows a zero-copy slice of the input, and only a token containing an escape allocates. This was weighed against two alternatives from the research phase:

* **Always-owned String.** Simplest and hardest to get wrong, at the cost of an allocation per identifier/string in every stylesheet. Reasonable as a *throwaway v0* while the tokenizer's happy-path shape is still being validated — introducing the 'i lifetime is mechanical but non-trivial, so deferring it to milestone 1 (Section 9\) is an acceptable sequencing choice, not a scope cut.

* **bumpalo arena allocation.** Attractive for AST *nodes* (many small, uniformly-lived allocations) but a poor fit for *strings* specifically, per the research phase's finding that arenas mainly pay off for node-heavy, not string-heavy, workloads. Tracked as a possible v2 optimization once profiling — not intuition — justifies it.

## **7.3 Error handling & recovery**

Errors are collected, not thrown: a Parser accumulates a Vec\<ParseError\> as it goes and keeps parsing, mirroring the spec's own philosophy that one bad rule shouldn't sink the stylesheet (§2.2). Every call site that needs to resync (a bad declaration, a bad prelude) shares one primitive instead of re-implementing skip-to-delimiter logic ad hoc:

pub enum ParseError {  
    UnexpectedToken { expected: &'static str, found: String, at: Span },  
    UnterminatedString { at: Span },  
    UnterminatedUrl { at: Span },  
    UnterminatedComment { at: Span },  
    InvalidDeclaration { at: Span },  
    EmptyQualifiedRulePrelude { at: Span },  
}  
   
impl\<'i\> Parser\<'i\> {  
    /// Shared resync primitive: consumes component values until \`stop\`  
    /// matches the current token (typically \`;\` or \`}\`) or EOF,  
    /// discarding everything consumed. Implements the “throw away the  
    /// rest of the construct” recovery rule from CSS Syntax §2.2.  
    fn consume\_until(\&mut self, stop: impl Fn(\&Token) \-\> bool) { .. }  
}

## **7.4 Prior art (reference, not a dependency)**

The following crates implement overlapping problems and are worth reading for edge cases this specification may have under-specified — particularly An+B corner cases and color-function syntax — without this project depending on them directly, since the goal is a self-contained implementation:

* cssparser — Servo/Mozilla's tokenizer \+ generic component-value parser; combines lexing and parsing in one pass. [docs.rs/cssparser](https://docs.rs/cssparser/) · [github.com/servo/rust-cssparser](https://github.com/servo/rust-cssparser)

* selectors — Servo's selector-matching engine; useful reference for combinator and An+B edge cases. [docs.rs/selectors](https://docs.rs/selectors/)

* Lexbor — a C, pool-allocator-based engine; useful reference for error-tolerant tokenizing behavior even though it's a different language.

# **8\. Scope Boundary: Feature Coverage Matrix**

This section itemizes the line drawn in Section 1.2 between goals and non-goals. Nothing here is a value judgment about what CSS “should” support — it is a statement of what this crate's v1 is responsible for getting right versus what is explicitly deferred.

## **8.1 In scope**

| Area | Covered |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tokenizer | All 18 token types, incl. bad-string / bad-url error tokens, full escape handling, numeric edge cases (“1e”, “.5”, “+.5e-3”) |
| Rules | Stylesheet, rule-list, qualified rules, at-rules in both statement and block form |
| Declarations | property: value \[\!important\]; custom properties (--x) with raw \<any-value\> capture |
| Nesting | Nested qualified rules and “&” inside style blocks (CSS Nesting Module) |
| Selectors | Type / class / id / universal / attribute, all four combinators, compound & complex lists, An+B |
| At-rule catalog | @media, @supports, @import, @font-face, @keyframes, @page, @layer, @container, @property — prelude and block parsed generically for all; contents interpreted only where noted above |
| Values | Numbers / dimensions / percentages / strings / urls, functions (incl. nested), calc() arithmetic (numeric), var() with fallback, comma/space-separated lists |
| Error recovery | The spec's panic-mode resync (§2.2): bad declarations skip to the next ; or }; bad preludes skip to the next , or the rule's end |

## **8.2 Out of scope (by design)**

| Area | Why it's excluded |
| :---- | :---- |
| Property-specific value grammars | Validating that e.g. color: only accepts a \<color\> is the job of each property's own defining spec, not the Syntax module |
| Full Selectors L4 semantics | :has() cycle/scoping rules, ::part() / ::slotted() shadow-tree interaction — matching semantics, not parsing |
| Unit-checked calc() | Only numeric-only arithmetic is evaluated structurally; mixing px and % correctly requires a type system this crate doesn't build |
| Condition evaluation | @supports / @media conditions are parsed structurally but never evaluated against a real environment |
| CSSOM / cascade | Specificity, inheritance, computed values, and the live DOM-facing object model are all out of scope |
| Legacy encoding detection | Beyond a BOM \+ @charset sniff, full charset-label fallback detection (§3.2) is not implemented; UTF-8 input is assumed |
| urange (unicode-range) | Only used by @font-face's unicode-range descriptor; tracked as a stretch goal, not required for v1 |
| Vendor/proprietary microsyntaxes | Fall through to the generic component-value representation rather than being specially parsed |

# **9\. Implementation Roadmap**

Milestones are ordered so that each one produces a runnable, testable increment; later milestones depend on the generic AST from milestones 1–4 but not on each other, so 5–8 can be reordered based on which CSS subset the consuming project needs first.

| \# | Milestone | Deliverable | Key refs | Difficulty |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Tokenizer foundation | All 18 token types \+ escapes, unit-tested against hand-written cases | §4 | Moderate |
| 2 | Rule skeleton | consume\_list\_of\_rules / at-rule / qualified rule producing the generic AST | §5.4.1–3 | Moderate |
| 3 | Declarations | consume\_declaration(\_list) incl. custom properties & \!important | §5.4.5–6 | Moderate |
| 4 | Component values | consume\_component\_value / simple\_block / function | §5.4.7–9 | Low–Moderate |
| 5 | Nesting | Style-block contents' dual declaration/rule dispatch | §5.4.4 \+ Nesting | Moderate–High |
| 6 | Selectors | Combinators, attribute selectors, compound/complex lists, An+B | Selectors L4 \+ §6 | Moderate |
| 7 | Values | calc() expression tree, var(), color functions, list separators | Values & Units L4 | High |
| 8 | At-rule catalog | @media/@supports/@import/@font-face/@keyframes/@page/@layer/@container/@property preludes | respective specs | Moderate |
| 9 | Error-recovery hardening | consume\_until resync applied uniformly; malformed-CSS fuzz corpus | §2.2 | Moderate |
| 10 | Test-suite integration | Wire up WPT css-syntax plus unit/property tests in CI | Section 10 | Ongoing |

# **10\. Testing & Validation Strategy**

## **10.1 Conformance tests**

The [web-platform-tests](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt) repository's css/css-syntax suite is the primary structural conformance oracle, since it exercises the exact tokenizer and parser algorithms this document implements (Sections 4–5) independent of any particular browser.

## **10.2 Unit tests**

* Per-token-type edge cases: unterminated strings/URLs/comments, invalid escapes, numeric edge cases (“1e”, “.5”, “+.5e-3”, bare “.”).

* Per-algorithm edge cases: an empty declaration, a declaration missing its colon, an at-rule with no block, unmatched brackets at EOF (which §2.2 requires to auto-close rather than error out).

## **10.3 Property-based & fuzz testing**

* proptest\-generated random token streams asserting the tokenizer and parser never panic, regardless of how malformed the input is.

* cargo-fuzz harness targeting parse\_stylesheet directly on arbitrary bytes (after UTF-8 repair), to catch panics, unbounded recursion, and pathological-input hangs.

## **10.4 Differential & round-trip checks**

* Reserialize the generic AST and re-parse it, asserting a stable fixpoint wherever the spec's “representation” concept (§4.2) makes one meaningful.

* Optional differential comparison of tokenization output against cssparser over a corpus of real-world stylesheets, as an informal parity signal — not a spec authority, since non-normative diagram-level details can legitimately differ between two independent, compliant implementations.
